item.title: An Efficient Quantum Spectral-Galerkin Method for Linear Elliptic Equations
item.description: arXiv:2610.33095v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents an efficient quantum spectral-Galerkin method for constant-coefficient second-order linear elliptic equations. The method employs a boundary-adapted Jacobi tensor-product basis that incorporates the boundary condition into the approximation space and produces Galerkin systems with polynomially bounded condition numbers and sparsity. For analytic solutions satisfying a suitable uniform regularity condition, spectral convergence allows the normalized Galerkin coefficient state to be prepared with complexity $\mathrm{poly}(d,\log(1/\epsilon))$, where $d$ is the spatial dimension and $\epsilon$ is the error tolerance, under standard sparse-access and state-preparation assumptions. At the state-preparation level, this improves the precision dependence over fixed-order finite-difference and finite-element discretizations. We further show how to estimate prescribed linear functionals of the solution, with an additional $O(1/\epsilon)$ factor arising from norm and inner-product estimation.
item.dc:creator: Dongjie Wang, Sheng Chen

item.title: Autonomous atomistic-continuum coupling through uncertainty-aware active learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.33272v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop an uncertainty-aware surrogate modeling approach for coupling an atomistic kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) surface-chemistry solver with a continuum multi-species fluid dynamics solver across disparate physical length and time scales. The surrogate model predicts boundary mass fluxes for six species and their uncertainties, which the continuum solver monitors to automatically trigger additional KMC simulations when new training data are needed. This enables efficient multiscale coupling and maintains a user-specified level of accuracy. We demonstrate the approach for reactive halide-perovskite vapor deposition, which involves a multi-species vapor jet impinging on a reactive substrate. The KMC solver uses a DFT-calibrated energetics model that we construct as part of this work and provides net deposition and desorption rates for six species. With a conservative uncertainty threshold, the surrogate-coupled approach reproduces cumulative mass fluxes of the directly coupled approach with errors typically within 10-20%, while capturing the non-monotonic dependence of net deposition on species partial pressure. Importantly, the results show that detailed crystal structure need not be explicitly represented to predict quantities exchanged between atomistic and continuum solvers; species-resolved mass fluxes provide a sufficiently low-dimensional representation of the atomistic response. For this accuracy target, the autonomous online-learning approach reduces the number of required atomistic simulations by two to three orders of magnitude relative to direct multiscale coupling.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Abdulah, Hariswaran Sitaraman, Ross E. Larsen, Kevin Patrick Griffin, Grace Wei, Janelle Domantay, Ethan Young, Marc T. Henry de Frahan

item.title: A neural accelerated surface-roughness-based Discrete Element Method (SR-DEM) for modeling granular systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.33363v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Discrete Element Method (DEM) is an indispensable tool for modeling and understanding the basic mechanical behaviors of (dry) granular media, a class of disordered material systems of significant interest to multiple scientific domains from (geo-)physics to (chemical) engineering. At the core of all present DEM frameworks is a phenomenological friction law--commonly chosen to be of the Amontons-Coulomb type--that models the frictional interaction among constituent grains. Here, inspired by research in the tribology community, we present an alternative, fundamentally different framework, termed surface-roughness-based DEM (SR-DEM), in which contact friction is handled in a more physics-based manner. In this framework, instead of using a friction law, we explicitly resolve the surface topography of each grain and let friction emerge from collective frictionless interactions of surface asperities. In essence, we trade phenomenology for physics at the cost of an increased computational demand. To mitigate the cost, we introduce an FE$^2$-like algorithm and a feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM)-based neural network surrogate, both of which are parallelized on GPU to accelerate contact computation. Crucially, using this framework in 2D, we (1) demonstrate the possibility of recovering a two-body-based Amontons-Coulomb-type friction behavior using a simple representation of surface topography, and (2) identify many-body-based frictional behaviors--more specifically, the angle of repose values--that cannot always be captured by current DEM frameworks under the same level of model complexity. We conclude by discussing future directions for SR-DEM, as well as exciting new opportunities it could unlock for a wide range of emerging applications, including (designing) suspension rheology and metamaterial mechanics.
item.dc:creator: Xiwei Pan, Liuchi Li

item.title: A Differentiable Framework for Inverse Identification of Heterogeneous Cohesive Laws
item.description: arXiv:2610.33711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work develops a differentiable finite element framework based on an intrinsic cohesive-zone formulation for identifying traction-separation laws from global force-displacement histories and spatially sparse strain measurements. The framework employs physics-constrained neural networks to represent flexible, thermodynamically structured cohesive laws, with sensitivities computed through automatic differentiation and a discrete adjoint that accounts for the history-dependent evolution of interfacial damage. To enable identification of spatially heterogeneous cohesive behavior, we extend learned constitutive priors to irreversible interfacial damage by constructing a shared, low-dimensional family of cohesive laws from representative traction-separation histories. This representation exploits common constitutive structure and parameter sharing to reduce the number of unknowns and regularize the inverse problem, while allowing local cohesive behavior to vary spatially through latent coordinates. Numerical investigations involving double-cantilever beams and fiber-matrix composites demonstrate that accurate reproduction of global force-displacement responses does not necessarily imply accurate recovery of the underlying cohesive laws. Incorporating spatially resolved strain measurements substantially improves constitutive identification, even when the admissible responses are constrained by a learned prior. Comparisons with conventional bilinear cohesive models and Bayesian optimization further illustrate the benefits of the learned constitutive representation and adjoint-based identification for high-dimensional inverse problems.
item.dc:creator: Sida Hao, Jinkyo Han, Bahador Bahmani

item.title: Two-dimensional framework for modeling load transfer in nanocomposites with thin, stiff, and prestressed reinforcements
item.description: arXiv:2610.34014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for simulating load-transfer mechanisms in nanocomposites reinforced by thin, stiff, and prestressed reinforcements, such as, e.g., nanosheets or nanoplatelets. The reinforcements are modeled as open material surfaces treated as membranes endowed with their own elastic properties and residual surface tension; the matrix is assumed to be isotropic elastic. In the two-dimensional plane-strain setting considered here, each material surface is represented by a sufficiently smooth curve of otherwise arbitrary shape. The theoretical part of the framework is based on the Gurtin--Murdoch theory in which the surfaces are represented by traction jumps across them. The elastic fields in the matrix are exactly expressed by the integral representations written in terms of the unknown traction jumps that are functions of the second-order derivatives of the displacements. The computational part is based on the isogeometric boundary element method (IGABEM) that utilizes non-uniform rational B-splines (NURBS). The unknown traction jumps are found from the numerical solutions of the coupled system of singular boundary integral equations, after which the elastic fields in the matrix are evaluated. The procedure of extracting the values of the stress intensity factors (SIFs) at the tips of the surfaces is described. The proposed algorithm is validated against available benchmark solutions for multiple surfaces located along either straight segments or circular arcs. Selected parametric studies are performed to examine the influence of surface curvatures, relative spacing, orientation, and interactions. An example involving a graphene nanoplatelet-reinforced epoxy is presented.
item.dc:creator: Rohit Satish Patil, Zhilin Han, Sofia G. Mogilevskaya

item.title: kstress: a LAMMPS package for calculating the 2D wavevector-dependent stress tensor and its anisotropy in amorphous solids
item.description: arXiv:2610.34206v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The stress tensor resolved in wavevector $\qvec$ and time $t$, $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\qvec,t)$, gives access to the elastic moduli of amorphous solids as a function of the probed length scale, and to the long-range stress correlations that distinguish an amorphous solid from a liquid. Its evaluation requires the contribution of every interacting pair and therefore an interface to the force loop of the molecular dynamics code. In the current work, we present: i) an optimized implementation of the LAMMPS~\cite{lammps} module for calculating $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\qvec,t)$, in which trigonometric functions are calculated only for the basic wavevectors and, in addition, all the relevant wavevectors are supplied as an explicit list rather than generated as a full grid, so that only the wavevectors of interest are computed and stored, and ii) a validation protocol for the code illustrated for a two-dimensional polydisperse Lennard-Jones (2DpLJ) glass-forming liquid. Based on these technical achievements we elucidated how the affine moduli for the 2DpLJ model depend on the norm $q$ of the wavevector. In particular, we demonstrate that the longitudinal affine modulus shows a minimum near $q_\text{max}$ corresponding to the main peak of the structure factor. Our data also point to the peaks in the $q$-dependencies of vibrational frequencies well below $q_\text{max}$ for both transverse and longitudinal modes. The potential relevance of this feature to the ``boson peak'' is discussed as well.
item.dc:creator: Olivier Benzerara, J\"org Baschnagel, Alexander N. Semenov, Liudmyla Klochko

item.title: A GPU-efficient local ADER finite-difference method for compressible-flow DNS
item.description: arXiv:2610.34252v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Algorithm design tailored to graphics processing units (GPUs) can substantially improve the efficiency of computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations. Efforts to adapt CFD solvers to GPUs often focus on spatial discretization, while time advancement commonly relies on multistage Runge--Kutta (RK) methods. However, these RK methods require repeated residual evaluations and full-domain operations, increasing the cost of compressible-flow direct numerical simulation (DNS). To reduce this overhead, we develop a local arbitrary high-order derivatives (ADER) finite-difference method that couples a compact ten-point quadratic predictor to a conservative central corrector through operator matching. With two quadrature nodes, one Picard correction, and selective dissipation, smooth convective tests recover third-order convergence under fixed-CFL refinement and near-seventh-order spatial behavior when background spatial error dominates. Temporal states remain kernel-local, and halo communication overlaps interior computation. Tests of smooth advection, periodic turbulence, and wall-bounded flows assess accuracy and flow statistics. On a $302^3$-node viscous Taylor--Green benchmark without heat conduction, throughput reaches 230.87 million node updates per second on one V100 GPU in double precision, 1.944 times that of spatially matched three-stage Runge--Kutta integration. Weak-scaling efficiency reaches 99.44\% from 4 to 32 V100 GPUs at 1.812 billion nodes.
item.dc:creator: Hong Zhang, Xian Wang, Xinliang Li, Yibing Chen, Xing Ji

item.title: Towards Exact Multidimensional Fluxes: A Structure-Preserving Data-Informed Framework for Riemann Solvers
item.description: arXiv:2610.35265v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finite-volume and discontinuous Galerkin methods update cells using the space-time flux integral over their faces, which typically depends on the solutions to local Riemann problems. In the multidimensional Riemann problem setting, this integral is difficult to evaluate exactly because of complex wave interactions. In this work, we show that the exact space-time flux integral is a polynomial in the time step and face dimensions. This motivates a learning-based approach, as only the mapping from the initial states to the polynomial coefficients needs to be learned. We propose a structure-preserving, data-informed Riemann solver framework that uses a neural network trained on high-resolution simulation data to learn this mapping. Key structural properties, including consistency and symmetry, are enforced by construction. Provided that the high-resolution simulations converge to the exact flux integrals and the network accurately predicts the coefficients, this framework yields near-exact flux integrals for use in numerical simulations. We demonstrate the framework using classical implosion and explosion problems for the two-dimensional Euler equations. In an unsplit MUSCL-Hancock scheme, the learned Riemann solver remains stable at a CFL number of 0.9, whereas the same scheme using the exact one-dimensional Riemann solver fails. Compared with the latter scheme at CFL=0.45, the learned scheme is slightly more accurate and requires approximately 30% less computational time.
item.dc:creator: Yucheng Zhang, Clint Dawson

item.title: Localized Hybrid Analytical-Finite-Element Thermal Modeling for Laser Powder Bed Fusion
item.description: arXiv:2610.33273v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hybrid analytical--finite-element methods support scan-resolved, part-scale thermal simulation of laser powder bed fusion, but their analytical evaluation cost grows as scan-line contributions accumulate. This work develops a space--time localized hybrid formulation that restricts where and how long each contribution is evaluated analytically. Residual terms and boundary conditions derived from the heat equation allow the finite-element correction to account for the thermal effect of contributions removed from the analytical field. The formulation is assessed using a single-line benchmark against an independent full finite-element solution and multiline comparisons with the conventional hybrid formulation. Localization limits the number of analytical contributions retained while maintaining close agreement with the conventional solution. A comparison with uncompensated temporal truncation demonstrates the importance of the residual correction in retaining the thermal effect of removed contributions. In the 500-line case, analytical and total simulation times are reduced by factors of approximately 25.5 and 3.92, respectively, with a relative nodal 2-norm difference of 0.139%.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Amin Mohammadi Golafshani, Krishnan Suresh

item.title: Resource competition and survival for random walkers on complex networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.33831v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider the problem of $W$ random walkers on a complex network where each walker requires an amount $\theta$ of resource at each time to survive. Resource is stochastically produced at each vertex of the network with a specified distribution. The survival time of the system of walkers is defined as the time required for all $W$ walkers to die. Using numerical simulations, we show that Erd{\H o}s-R\'enyi networks a have higher mean survival time than Scale-free networks as expected, but also that uniform distribution production leads to higher mean survival time than exponential distribution with the same mean. We derive an exact expression for the survival-time distribution under the assumption of independent walker lifespans, and use it to show that scale-free network topology produces strong dependence in the lifespans but homogeneous topology does not. We moreover demonstrate how the survival time can be substantially increased without changing the resource production or network topology by appropriately biasing the movement of the walkers towards low degree vertices on Scale-free networks, but has no effect on Erd{\H o}s-R{\'e}nyi networks.
item.dc:creator: Snehal Shekatkar

item.title: Symmetry-driven in-situ physical adjoint computing beyond reciprocity
item.description: arXiv:2610.34637v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Nonreciprocity enriches wave control and information processing through directional transport, yet challenges conventional in-situ physical adjoint optimization, which relies on reciprocity to acquire adjoint responses. Here we demonstrate symmetry-driven in-situ physical adjoint computing (Sym-iPAC) in nonreciprocal systems, which enables access to adjoint responses on the original hardware through three classes of transpose symmetry: local geometric permutations, complex gauge reweighting, and latent symmetry in effective port dynamics revealed by Schur reduction. Experiments with programmable nonreciprocal microwave networks validate these transpose relations and yield adjoint gradients, enabling closed-loop optimization. These results establish experimentally accessible transpose symmetry as a route to in-situ physical adjoint computing beyond reciprocity.
item.dc:creator: Cunshen Li, Rong Li, Jiongning Che, Cheng-Zhen Wang, Liang Huang

item.title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for coupled stiff transport systems
item.description: arXiv:2606.21236v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN) struggle with stiff, regime-changing transport equations due to instability, loss imbalance, and violations of physical consistency. This paper investigates these failures through the Marshak wave equations, a canonical benchmark from radiative transport, where initial and boundary conditions differ by up to 12 orders of magnitude, and proposes modifications to the standard PINN framework to overcome them. Three modifications are introduced: a ScaledSigmoid final activation enforcing physical bounds and positivity of the unknowns; a logarithmic MSE loss replacing the standard quadratic loss for initial and boundary conditions, enabling training across extreme scale disparities; and explicit enforcement of global conservation laws as an additional physics loss term. Monte Carlo sampling with exponential time weighting is used throughout. The proposed framework recovers the Marshak wave dynamics - including the hot, cold, and wave-front regions - in good agreement with a reference Implicit Monte Carlo solution (sub-millimeter absolute error on the front position, although the relative error remains substantial at early times), with run times under 5 minutes. Ablation studies confirm that each ingredient is essential: linear activation, absence of the logarithmic loss, or removal of the PDE term each independently cause the method to fail qualitatively. This work identifies and resolves three concrete failure modes of standard PINN on stiff hyperbolic systems with nonlinear coupling. The combination of bounded activations, scale-aware loss functions, and conservation law enforcement constitutes a framework validated on the present one-dimensional Marshak wave problem, with potential extension to other coupled stiff transport systems in engineering.
item.dc:creator: Laetitia Laguzet, Gabriel Turinici

item.title: Machine learning kinetics from molecular dynamics data
item.description: arXiv:2609.17736v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Most molecular transitions occur on time scales far beyond direct molecular dynamics simulations. The committor, the probability that a configuration reaches a product state before a reactant state, is a central kinetic statistic, providing a mechanism-independent reaction coordinate and a foundation for transition path theory and the calculation of rates. This review surveys modern approaches for estimating the committor and related kinetic statistics from molecular simulations, with an emphasis on self-supervised methods that learn solutions of their defining dynamical equations rather than relying on labeled shooting data. We develop a common operator viewpoint connecting generator-based partial differential equations, variational principles, Markov state models, dynamical Galerkin approximation, and neural networks. Empirical and theoretical evidence points to the efficiency of these methods. We provide theoretical and practical guidance for realizing their full potential in applications, including strategies for treating non-Markovian effects and for sampling. We conclude by identifying opportunities for further research, including connections to reinforcement learning and generative modeling.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Weare, Aaron R. Dinner

item.title: Matrix-Free Resolvent Analysis for Large-Scale Aerodynamic Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.26931v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Predicting transonic buffet requires resolving both flow stability and disturbance amplification. Resolvent analysis gives the amplification. However, each gain needs the solution of tens of linear systems with the shifted Jacobian and its adjoint. Sparse direct factorization, the usual route, is extrapolated to need more than $130$ TB for a three-dimensional jet with $4\times 10^{7}$ unknowns. For the stiff Reynolds-averaged operator of a transonic wing, iterative solution has been reported to stall on the adjoint system. To avoid the direct factorization and to converge the adjoint, we present a matrix-free resolvent framework in the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes solver ADflow that combines automatic differentiation, Krylov solution with subspace recycling, and Lanczos bidiagonalization, with backward-error checks on each singular triplet. A three-level study of the NASA Common Research Model wing reaches $1.73\times 10^{8}$ complex unknowns. The coarsest grid predicts an unstable buffet mode, whereas no unstable eigenvalue is found on the finer grids within the shifts searched. The finer-grid gain peaks are consistent with collective amplification by damped modes, whose responses retain the buffet-cell structure and travel outboard at approximately $0.3$ of the free-stream speed. The peak gain remains sensitive to resolution despite these similar structures. These findings motivate future mesh adaptation targeted at convergence of flow stability and disturbance amplification.
item.dc:creator: Rohit Sunil Kanchi, Sicheng He

item.title: Compressing multivariate functions with tree tensor networks
item.description: arXiv:2410.03572v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tensor networks are a compressed format for multi-dimensional data. One dimensional tensor networks -- often referred to as tensor trains (TT) or matrix product states (MPS) -- are increasingly being used as a numerical ansatz for continuum functions by ``quantizing'' the inputs into discrete binary digits. Here we demonstrate the power of more general tree tensor networks (TTNs) for this purpose. We provide direct constructions of a number of elementary functions as generic tree tensor networks and interpolative constructions for more complicated functions via a generalization of the tensor cross interpolation algorithm. For a range of multi-dimensional functions we show how more structured tree tensor networks offer a significantly more efficient ansatz than the commonly used tensor train. Finally, we demonstrate how the methods introduced in this work can be used to realize a TTN-based solver for multi-dimensional, non-linear Fredholm equations.
item.dc:creator: Joseph Tindall, E. Miles Stoudenmire, Ryan Levy

item.title: Revealing the proton slingshot mechanism in solid acid electrolytes through machine learning molecular dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2503.15389v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In solid acid electrolytes CsH$_2$PO$_4$ and CsHSO$_4$, the origin of fast proton conduction has long been debated, attributed either to local proton hopping or to polyanion rotation. However, the precise role of polyanion rotation and its interplay with proton hopping remained unresolved. Nanosecond-scale molecular dynamics simulations, driven by equivariant neural network force fields, reveal a nuanced proton slingshot mechanism: protons are first carried by rotating polyanions, followed by O-H bond reorientation, and the combined motion enables long-range jumps. This mechanism challenges the conventional revolving paddlewheel model, revealing long-range transport arises from significant O-H bond reorientation assisted by only limited polyanion rotation. Despite their structural similarity, CsH$_2$PO$_4$ and CsHSO$_4$ exhibit qualitatively different transport behavior, governed by their distinct proton concentrations. In CsH$_2$PO$_4$, two rotation rates with different activation energies emerge, while CsHSO$_4$ displays a single-rate process with faster productive polyanion dynamics. The higher proton concentration in CsH$_2$PO$_4$ frustrates PO$_4$ rotation, resulting in slower dynamics than for SO$_4$ in CsHSO$_4$. In CsH$_2$PO$_4$, we further identify a unique correlation between oxygen sharing and proton transport, arising from the extra proton per polyanion. Together, our findings establish a unified framework linking polyanion rotation, proton coordination, and long-range transport, and suggest that tuning proton concentration could accelerate rotation and enhance conductivity.
item.dc:creator: Menghang Wang, Jingxuan Ding, Grace Xiong, Ni Zhan, Cameron J. Owen, Albert Musaelian, Yu Xie, Nicola Molinari, Ryan P. Adams, Sossina Haile, Boris Kozinsky

item.title: When Does Cheap Physics Help? Gated Multi-Fidelity Physics-Informed Networks with Provable Sample Savings and Conformal Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2602.01176v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: High-fidelity (HF) simulations of parametric partial differential equations are expensive, whereas low-fidelity (LF) models such as coarse grids or simplified physics are cheap but biased. Multi-fidelity physics-informed neural networks combine the two, yet it remains unclear when cheap physics actually reduces the number of HF solves, and existing methods silently fail when the LF model is misleading and offer no guaranteed uncertainty. We answer the first question with a sharp sample-complexity bound: learning the HF field through its discrepancy from the LF model reduces the number of HF samples needed for accuracy $\varepsilon$ by the factor $\kappa^{2\gamma}$, where $\kappa$ is the ratio of the complexity of the discrepancy to that of the HF field and $\gamma$ is the effective-dimension exponent, and we confirm the predicted scaling with exact risk computations in a kernel model. Guided by the analysis, we propose GaMF-PINN, a gated multi-fidelity PINN that learns where to trust the LF model and falls back to physics-only learning where it does not, together with a function-level conformal procedure that returns uncertainty bands containing the entire HF solution with probability at least $1-\alpha$ in finite samples. We release MFPDE-Bench, an open benchmark of paired LF/HF solvers for four parametric PDEs with coarse-grid and simplified-physics LF models. Across MFPDE-Bench, GaMF-PINN reaches the accuracy of a standard HF-PINN with up to 8x fewer HF solves, remains robust when the LF model is deliberately corrupted, and attains the nominal coverage where Bayesian PINNs and deep ensembles under-cover.
item.dc:creator: Olaf Yunus Laitinen Imanov, Rana Irem Turhan, Isgandar Jafarli

item.title: A Stable, High-Order Time-Stepping Scheme for the Drift-Diffusion Model in Modern Solar Cell Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2603.09063v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper presents a one-dimensional transient drift-diffusion simulator for advanced solar cells, integrating a structure-preserving finite-volume spatial discretization with Scharfetter-Gummel-type fluxes and a high-order, L-stable implicit Runge-Kutta (Radau IIA) temporal integrator. The scheme ensures local charge conservation, handles sharp material interfaces, achieves second-order spatial and fifth-order temporal convergence, and exhibits excellent computational efficiency and numerical stability. Its accuracy is verified against the classical depletion approximation in p-n junction and validated against four independent software implementations for an organic photovoltaic device under a common protocol. The framework's extensibility is demonstrated by incorporating exciton kinetics in organic solar cells, capturing multi-timescale dynamics, and by modeling mobile ions in perovskite solar cells, reproducing characteristic J-V hysteresis without empirical parameters. This work provides a robust, high-order numerical foundation for simulating coupled charge, exciton, and ion transport in next-generation photovoltaic devices.
item.dc:creator: Jun Du, Jun Yan

item.title: High-order kernel regularization of singular and hypersingular Helmholtz boundary integral operators
item.description: arXiv:2604.14797v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper extends and analyzes the high-order kernel regularization framework of Beale & Tlupova (arXiv:2510.13639) to all four on-surface boundary integral operators of the Helmholtz Calderon calculus in three dimensions: the single-layer, double-layer, adjoint double-layer, and hypersingular operators. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first high-order kernel regularization of the hypersingular operator for both the Helmholtz and Laplace equations in three dimensions. The regularization replaces each singular kernel with a smooth modification constructed from error functions together with a polynomial correction whose coefficients are determined through moment conditions. Alongside the derivation of the regularizing functions, the paper provides a unified error analysis of the combined regularization and quadrature discretization procedure. By coupling the regularization parameter to the mesh size, the two error contributions can be balanced, leading to explicit overall convergence rates that depend jointly on the order of the regularization and the degree of exactness of the surface quadrature rule. A key practical feature of the method is its implementation simplicity. Once the regularizing functions are determined, the numerical task reduces entirely to the evaluation of smooth surface integrals using standard quadrature, without the need for element-local solves, singularity-specific precomputations, or specialized quadrature rules. Although the modified kernel is generally incompatible with kernel-specific fast methods, this limitation is addressed through H-matrix acceleration, applicable in a black-box manner. Numerical examples -- including verification of the predicted convergence rates and solution of sound-soft and sound-hard scattering problems by smooth obstacles -- demonstrate the accuracy and practicality of the proposed methodology.
item.dc:creator: Luiz M. Faria, Carlos Perez-Arancibia, Svetlana Tlupova

item.title: CrystalREPA: Transferring Physical Priors from Universal MLIPs to Crystal Generative Models
item.description: arXiv:2605.08960v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Crystal generative models mainly learn what stable crystals look like, with little explicit supervision for what makes them stable. We reveal a substantial representation gap between state-of-the-art crystal generative models and pretrained universal machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) via energy probing, and show this gap can be closed by a simple training-time alignment. We propose Crystal REPresentation Alignment (CrystalREPA), a plug-and-play framework that aligns the atom-wise hidden states of generative encoders with frozen MLIP representations through an element-aware contrastive objective, transferring stability-aware atomistic priors with marginal training overhead and no additional inference cost. Across three generative frameworks, ten MLIP teachers, and two benchmark datasets, CrystalREPA consistently improves the thermodynamic stability, structural validity, and structural fidelity of generated crystals. Equally important, we find that an MLIP's transfer effectiveness is poorly predicted by its accuracy on standard leaderboards (e.g., Matbench Discovery) but strongly predicted by the distinguishability of its atom-wise representation space, yielding a practical, accuracy-independent criterion for selecting MLIP teachers for generative transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/Chengqian-Zhang/CrystalREPA.
item.dc:creator: Chengqian Zhang, Yucheng Jin, Duo Zhang, Tiejun Li, Han Wang

item.title: First-Principles Wannier Representation of Proximity Effects
item.description: arXiv:2607.25690v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Proximity effects in layered heterostructures are commonly represented by static parameters fitted to first-principles band structures, an approximation that usually discards the energy dependence of interlayer hybridization, momentum transfer, and spatial structure. We address this limitation by deriving a dynamical proximity operator directly from density functional theory by downfolding the heterostructure Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian onto a fixed low-energy target Wannier subspace. We demonstrate the method for three different graphene heterostructures coupled to magnetic and semiconducting substrates. Graphene/hBN/Co(0001) exhibits proximity-induced exchange resonances driven by hybridization with Co states. Graphene/PtSe$_2$ develops a sublattice-selective, intervalley-coherent, proximity-induced coupling. For graphene/WSe$_2$, we identify the spatial modulation of both Rashba and valley-Zeeman proximity-induced spin-orbit couplings. The method determines the full microscopic structure of the proximity coupling from first principles, providing input for transport and correlated-phase calculations.
item.dc:creator: Yaroslav Zhumagulov, Johan F\'elisaz, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Denis Kochan, Oleg V. Yazyev

item.title: An Energy-Based Conservative-Dissipative Latent Neural Evolution Operator for Magnetization Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2609.04530v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce a reduced-order learning framework that couples a convolutional autoencoder to a structured latent neural ordinary differential equation. A learned scalar generates the latent dynamics through an antisymmetric operator and a positive-definite dissipative operator. The antisymmetric component permits motion along scalar level sets, while the dissipative component decreases the scalar. Adding a coercive quadratic term gives bounded continuous-time latent trajectories and approach to the scalar's critical set under the stated assumptions. The scalar provides a structural constraint rather than an approximation of physical energy. The encoder, decoder, scalar, and operators are trained jointly on short snapshot windows without time-derivative supervision, physical-energy labels, or dissipation penalties. At inference, one initial state is encoded and evolved continuously in latent space, with decoding only at requested times. We demonstrate the framework on micromagnetic magnetization trajectories from NIST $\mu$MAG Standard Problem 4 and compare it with dissipative-only dynamics and an unstructured latent neural differential equation. Repeated training runs show competitive observed-horizon accuracy, while selected longer rollouts illustrate improved retention of approximately stationary states relative to the unstructured baseline. These results motivate scalar-generated latent dynamics as an inductive bias for reduced-order prediction and other learning tasks where bounded evolution and equilibrium behavior are important.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Schaffer, Lukas Exl

item.title: FUSION: a skill-based research agent for publicly obtainable nuclear-physics codes
item.description: arXiv:2609.04742v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Running an unfamiliar nuclear-physics code is rarely difficult because of the physics alone. One must find and build the program, learn its input conventions, and decide whether a plausible output is actually correct. A general-purpose coding agent helps with the first two tasks but may make the last one harder: it can write an input file that runs with the wrong physical convention. FUSION addresses this problem with code-specific skills. A skill obtains the code from its public source, starts from a verified input, runs and parses the calculation, records known failure modes, and must reproduce a stated benchmark to a stated tolerance before reporting a result. The current release covers twenty codes, spanning optical models and reactions, nuclear structure, fission and statistical models, astrophysics and R-matrix analysis, and heavy-ion transport. It also includes an offline, searchable collection of 61 167 pages derived from the nucl-th literature. User notes and credentials remain outside the public repository. FUSION is available under the MIT license at https://github.com/jinleiphys/FUSION; documentation is at https://vibeinscience.com. Here I describe the design, the checks behind the current release, and one complete calculation from input to comparison with measured data.
item.dc:creator: Jin Lei

item.title: Shannon Entropy as an Order Parameter for the Two-Dimensional Confined Coulomb Systems: Exact Balance Law, Topological Charge Sum Rule, and Boundary Saturation
item.description: arXiv:2609.15428v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We establish a complete information-theoretic framework for the minimum-energy configurations of the two-dimensional Thomson problem on a hard-wall disk, based on the Shannon entropy of the Voronoi topological charge distribution. Two exact identities are proven and verified to machine precision for all studied systems of size $N=12-10^5$. First, an entropy balance law decomposes the total entropy into bulk, boundary, and mixing contributions without approximation. Second, a topological charge sum rule fixes the total charge at twice the number of boundary particles plus six; together with the disjointness of bulk and boundary coordination sets $-$ justified analytically via the Delaunay empty-circumcircle criterion and elastic disclination splitting $-$ it relates the three- and four-coordinated boundary populations directly to the bulk charge. Applying Euler's theorem to the outermost Delaunay annulus yields an exact shell-mismatch identity: the four-coordinated boundary population equals the adjacent interior shell population, whereas the three-coordinated population equals their step mismatch, directly detecting third-shell nucleation at $N=30$. Furthermore, we prove that the boundary entropy is bounded by $\ln2$ and that its saturation is equivalent to the bulk charge per boundary particle approaching $-1/2$, a regime restricted self-consistently to boundaries of at least $12$ particles. Numerically, we locate bulk nucleation at $N=56$, maximal global disorder at $N=146$, and boundary saturation above $N\sim10^3$, with a direct extension to spherical geometry.

item.title: Femtosecond Three-Dimensional Imaging of Single-Protein with Hard X-ray Laser
item.description: arXiv:2610.11892v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The extreme intensity of X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL) pulses has enabled imaging of radiation-sensitive samples, such as macromolecular microcrystals, beyond radiation damage limits. These sources have the potential to enable biomolecular single-particle imaging, similar to cryo-electron microscopy but without the need for cryo-fixation and with temporal resolution from femtoseconds to milliseconds. While this possibility was recognized before XFELs were built, the biological single-particle imaging work flow has previously only been demonstrated on large virus particles. Building on improvements in X-ray beam focusing, particle delivery, diffraction detection, and advanced analysis, here we demonstrate imaging of a single molecular complex, the giant-hemoglobin erythrocruorin (Ery) with X-ray laser pulses. Two-dimensional classes of diffraction patterns could be reconstructed to 15 Angstrom resolution, and 3D images to ~20 to 30 Angstrom, even though the 3D merged intensity in reciprocal space extended beyond 20 Angstrom. The resolution discrepancy is likely due to heterogeneity caused by gas-phase compaction of the complexes. With increased throughput, this approach could be used to reveal in-situ structural details during mass spectrometry studies of biomolecules, while improvements in sample delivery may provide ultrafast snapshot imaging of biological single-particles in their native-state beyond the limitations of radiation damage.
